entries.title: MOLA topography
entries.summary: Global elevation of Mars, 3.7 km per pixel.
body: Height of the surface above the MOLA areoid, from the laser altimeter on Mars Global Surveyor. Each pixel is the median of the laser shots inside a 1/16-degree bin. It is the only elevation that covers the whole planet, so the Profile tool falls back to it wherever no finer DEM exists.
One 3.7 km pixel averages a crater rim and its floor together, so near Jezero MOLA reads about -1952 m where the 1 m DTM spans -2079 to -1758 m.

entries.title: TES albedo
entries.summary: How bright the ground is, whole planet, 7.4 km per pixel.
body: Lambert albedo (bolometric) from the Thermal Emission Spectrometer. Bright means dusty, dark means basaltic sand or rock. Values run from about 0.06 to 0.32. It is the layer to compare against elevation or thermal inertia to see whether dust or rock controls a pattern.

entries.title: Viking colour
entries.summary: Colour picture of the whole planet, 7.4 km per pixel.
body: The Viking Orbiter MDIM 2.1 colour mosaic. The original is 925 m per pixel; the explorer averages 8 x 8 blocks to 7.4 km. It is an image, not a measurement: use it as a basemap. Values shown in the Probe are grey level (0-255), and 0 is treated as no data.

entries.title: CTX image 12 m
entries.summary: Grey-scale photo of the Jezero region, 12 m per pixel.
body: The Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation CTX orthoimage mosaic (the original is 6 m per pixel; the explorer keeps every second pixel). 'Ortho' means it has been corrected for terrain so it sits correctly on the map. Covers 77.16-77.70 E, 18.21-18.72 N.

entries.title: CTX DTM 20 m
entries.summary: Elevation of the Jezero region, 20 m per pixel.
body: A digital terrain model from CTX stereo pairs, on the same areoid as the HiRISE DTM. It bridges the gap between 3.7 km MOLA and 1 m HiRISE: at the patch it reads -1798 m against HiRISE -1795 m. Profiles use it inside its footprint and drop to MOLA outside, so a profile jumps from 20 m to 3.7 km detail at the edge.

entries.title: THEMIS thermal inertia
entries.summary: How fast the ground heats and cools, 100 m per pixel.
body: Thermal inertia from the Mars Odyssey THEMIS camera (mosaic by Edwards & Buz 2021) over an 89 x 89 km area around Jezero. Low values are fine dust and sand, high values are rock and bedrock. The patch layer ('Thermal Inertia (4 m grid)') is a window of this same mosaic.
On the patch it runs 164 to 357 TIU. The rover's own MEDA sensor measured 180 (sand) to 605 (bedrock) at metre scale, so 100 m pixels that average both are in the expected range.

entries.title: CRISM Hydration (BD1900_2)
entries.summary: Water-bearing minerals, from the 1.9 micron band.
body: Depth of the 1.9 micron water absorption band. A higher value means more hydrated minerals (clays, sulfates, hydrated silica). Archive values, not clipped: a value at or below 0 means the absorption band is not there. A pixel is 181 m, so it averages many rock and sand surfaces; it cannot pick out single outcrops. On the patch the signal is weak, 0 to 0.036, as expected from a dusty, multispectral product. The patch version 'Hydrated Minerals' is the same data clipped at 0.

entries.title: CRISM Fe/Mg phyllosilicate (D2300)
entries.summary: Iron/magnesium clays, from the 2.3 micron drop-off.
body: Measures the drop in reflectance near 2.3 microns that Fe/Mg clays (smectites such as nontronite or saponite) cause. Clays form where rock sat in liquid water, which makes them a target for ancient-habitability work. Archive values, not clipped: a value at or below 0 means the absorption band is not there. A pixel is 181 m, so it averages many rock and sand surfaces; it cannot pick out single outcrops.

entries.title: CRISM Carbonate (BD2500_2)
entries.summary: Carbonate minerals, from the 2.5 micron band.
body: Depth of the 2.5 micron band: carbonates, which form in water and trap carbon dioxide. Carbonate-bearing rock is known along the inner rim of Jezero's neighbourhood and is a key sampling target. Archive values, not clipped: a value at or below 0 means the absorption band is not there. A pixel is 181 m, so it averages many rock and sand surfaces; it cannot pick out single outcrops. On the patch the values are all negative (-0.067 to -0.028), so there is no carbonate band at this resolution.

entries.title: CRISM Olivine (OLINDEX3)
entries.summary: Olivine, from the broad 1 micron band.
body: Index for olivine, an iron-magnesium silicate that weathers quickly in water, so finding it means the rock stayed dry or young. Jezero has a well known olivine-rich unit. Values here run 0.06 to 0.29 and are above 0 everywhere, so this is the strongest of the six CRISM signals. Archive values, not clipped: a value at or below 0 means the absorption band is not there. A pixel is 181 m, so it averages many rock and sand surfaces; it cannot pick out single outcrops.

entries.title: CRISM Low-Ca pyroxene (LCPINDEX2)
entries.summary: Low-calcium pyroxene (a dark volcanic mineral).
body: Index built from the 1.0 and 1.9 micron bands. Low-calcium pyroxene (orthopyroxene) is common in ancient volcanic crust. Archive values, not clipped: a value at or below 0 means the absorption band is not there. A pixel is 181 m, so it averages many rock and sand surfaces; it cannot pick out single outcrops.

entries.title: CRISM High-Ca pyroxene (HCPINDEX2)
entries.summary: High-calcium pyroxene (a volcanic mineral).
body: Index built from the 1.05 and 2.3 micron bands. High-calcium pyroxene (clinopyroxene) is typical of younger basaltic lava. Comparing it with the low-Ca layer separates old crust from younger lava. Archive values, not clipped: a value at or below 0 means the absorption band is not there. A pixel is 181 m, so it averages many rock and sand surfaces; it cannot pick out single outcrops.

entries.title: HiRISE DTM 1 m
entries.summary: Elevation of the 2 km patch, 1 m per pixel.
body: The finest elevation layer: the USGS Mars 2020 TRN HiRISE DTM mosaic cut to the patch (2000 x 2108 px). It ranges from -2079 m to -1758 m. It can be hillshaded, and it is what Profile uses whenever it is available.

entries.title: Slope 1 m
entries.summary: How steep the ground is, in degrees, 1 m per pixel.
body: Central-difference slope computed from the 1 m DTM. 0 degrees is flat. The EVA planner treats 20 degrees as a hard walking limit (never entered) and 15 degrees as a caution level. On the patch the slope is up to 43 degrees, and the 2nd to 98th percentile range is 4 to 28.

entries.title: Sky view
entries.summary: How much open sky a spot sees (1 = all of it).
body: The fraction of the sky dome not blocked by terrain, from the horizon angles of the HiRISE DTM. In a gully or at the foot of a cliff it is lower. It matters because rock overhead shields the radiation that falls from the sky; the dose model multiplies by it. On the patch it is 0.87 to 1.00.

entries.title: Roughness
entries.summary: How broken-up the ground is, scaled 0 to 1.
body: A terrain roughness index computed from the HiRISE DTM and scaled 0 to 1 (higher is rougher). It feeds the route cost: rough ground is slower and riskier to walk. The exact formula lives in the Marswalk web project's build_terrain.py, which is not in this repository, so it is documented here only by its range (0.01 to 1.0).

entries.title: Dose Rate (quiet)
entries.summary: Modelled radiation an astronaut would absorb per day.
body: Not a measurement: Perseverance carries no dosimeter. It is a model (see 'Radiation dose model') evaluated on the 4 m grid. Air above is thinner at higher ground, so the dose rises with elevation, and falls where the sky is partly blocked. The whole patch spans only 0.669 to 0.716 mSv/day.

entries.title: HiRISE image
entries.summary: Sharp photo of the 2 km patch (about 1 m per pixel here).
body: The HiRISE orthoimage of the patch (25 cm per pixel in the original), resampled to 2048 px across. Use it to see boulders, ripples and outcrops that the elevation layers smooth over.

entries.title: Patch layers on the 4 m grid
entries.summary: Slope, minerals, thermal, dose, ... resampled onto the web app's planning grid.
body: Every layer whose name ends in '(4 m grid)' comes from data/processed/layers.bin: the web app's own planning grid of 527 x 500 cells (3.80 x 4.00 m). Coarse data such as CRISM (181 m) or THEMIS (100 m) is resampled bilinearly, so each source pixel covers many cells and the picture is blocky. That is the data, not a bug. The regional CRISM and THEMIS layers show the same numbers at their true pixel size.

entries.title: HiRISE
entries.summary: Highest-resolution camera at Mars (25 cm per pixel).
body: High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO). From its stereo images USGS built the 1 m DTM and the 25 cm orthoimage used for the patch. Credit: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona, USGS.

entries.title: CTX
entries.summary: Context Camera on MRO (about 6 m per pixel).
body: The wide-view grey-scale camera on MRO. Its images cover the Jezero region at 6 m; stereo pairs give the 20 m DTM. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS, USGS.

entries.title: CRISM
entries.summary: MRO's mineral-mapping spectrometer.
body: Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars. It splits reflected sunlight into hundreds of colours, and minerals absorb light at tell-tale wavelengths. This project uses the multispectral reduced data record (MRDR) tile T1250 (72 channels, 181 m per pixel), not a targeted full-resolution scene. The targeted scenes over the Jezero delta start about 2 km east of the patch, so this tile is the only CRISM product covering it. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/JHU-APL.

entries.title: THEMIS
entries.summary: Mars Odyssey's thermal-infrared camera.
body: Thermal Emission Imaging System on the 2001 Mars Odyssey orbiter. Measuring how the ground's temperature changes through the day gives thermal inertia. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Arizona State University; mosaic by C. S. Edwards and J. Buz (Northern Arizona University), CC BY 4.0.

entries.title: MOLA (laser altimeter)
entries.summary: Mars Global Surveyor's laser that measured the planet's heights.
body: The Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter fired pulses at the surface and timed the echo. Its gridded product (MEGDR) is the global elevation here. Credit: NASA/GSFC, MGS MOLA team.

entries.title: TES
entries.summary: Thermal Emission Spectrometer on Mars Global Surveyor.
body: Measures infrared emission and reflected light. Its bolometric albedo mosaic (7.4 km per pixel) is the global 'how bright' layer. Credit: NASA/JPL/ASU, USGS.

entries.title: Viking Orbiter
entries.summary: 1970s orbiters whose pictures make the global colour map.
body: The Viking 1 and 2 orbiters photographed Mars in 1976-1980. The MDIM 2.1 mosaic is built from those pictures (USGS Astrogeology). Credit: NASA/JPL/USGS.

entries.title: MEDA
entries.summary: Perseverance's weather station.
body: Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer. Its thermal-infrared sensor (TIRS) gives air and ground temperature and a derived surface pressure. The explorer's Weather tab shows the median per local hour over sols 1349-1368, and the radiation model takes its pressure from it. No wind data exists for these sols. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/CAB(CSIC-INTA).

entries.title: MMGIS waypoints
entries.summary: NASA's list of where each rover stopped.
body: Multi-Mission Geographic Information System, the NASA web map. Its waypoint files give each rover's position, elevation and odometry per drive. The explorer's rover tracks and the five stops come from it. Positions are waypoints of the drive, not a continuous GPS trace.

entries.title: Areoid (elevation zero)
entries.summary: The reference surface all elevations are measured from.
body: Mars has no sea level. The areoid is an equal-gravity surface chosen as zero, so 'elevation -1800 m' means 1800 m below it. Jezero's floor is far below zero; Olympus Mons reaches about +21 km (the global layer's display range is -5.1 to +4.7 km, the 2nd to 98th percentile).

entries.title: DEM / DTM
entries.summary: A grid of elevation values.
body: Digital elevation model (DEM) and digital terrain model (DTM) are used interchangeably here: a raster where each pixel is a height. Layers that can be hillshaded and used by Profile are DEMs: MOLA, CTX DTM, HiRISE DTM.

entries.title: Orthoimage
entries.summary: A photo corrected so it lines up with the map.
body: Raw orbital pictures are distorted by terrain and viewing angle. An orthoimage has been warped using a DTM so distances measured on it are true.

entries.title: Hillshade and relief
entries.summary: Shading that makes elevation look 3D.
body: A simulated sun (from the north-west, 315 degrees azimuth, 45 degrees high) lights the DEM so slopes facing it are bright and others dark. The shading is computed in true metres for the latitude. 'relief x N' is a vertical exaggeration: it starts at 1 for pixels of 20 m or less and grows with pixel size (global topography would look flat otherwise), up to 30. You can type your own.

entries.title: Band depth and absorption
entries.summary: How deeply a mineral dims light at a specific colour.
body: Minerals absorb sunlight at particular wavelengths. Band depth is the fraction of light lost at the band centre compared with a straight-line continuum drawn across it. 0 means no band, 0.03 means 3% dimmer. The CRISM layers are all band depths or indices built from them.

entries.title: Summary parameters
entries.summary: Ready-made mineral indicators from CRISM data.
body: Viviano-Beck et al. (2014) defined a set of simple band-depth formulas that flag minerals (BD1900_2, D2300, BD2500_2, OLINDEX3, LCPINDEX2, HCPINDEX2, ...). The archive publishes them as maps. Values are archive values: they are not rescaled, and zero or below means the band is absent.

entries.title: Thermal inertia
entries.summary: How strongly the ground resists changing temperature.
body: Dust and fine sand heat up by day and cool down by night (low inertia). Solid rock changes slowly (high). The unit is TIU (thermal inertia unit) = J m-2 K-1 s-1/2. Rough guide: under about 200 is dust or sand, over about 400 is rock. It matters to astronauts for ground temperature and for choosing firm footing.

entries.title: Albedo
entries.summary: Fraction of sunlight the ground reflects.
body: 0 is perfectly dark, 1 is a perfect mirror. Bright Martian regions are covered in dust; dark ones are bare basaltic sand and rock. Lambert albedo assumes the ground scatters light evenly in all directions.

entries.title: Slope, walking limit and caution level
entries.summary: Steepness in degrees and what the planner allows.
body: Slope is the angle of the ground from horizontal, from 0 (flat) to 90 (a wall). The Marswalk planner never routes through cells steeper than 20 degrees (no-go) and flags 15 to 20 as caution.

entries.title: Radiation dose model
entries.summary: How the dose layer's numbers are calculated.
body: dose (mSv/day) = (220 + k x (840 - P)) x 3.05 / 1000 x sky view, where P is the surface pressure in Pa and k = 0.28 - 0.00029 x 600 = 0.106. The 220 uGy/day at 840 Pa is the dose rate Curiosity's RAD instrument measured at Gale (Guo et al. 2017); the atmosphere shields cosmic rays, so lower pressure raises the dose. 3.05 is the quality factor (Hassler et al. 2014) that turns absorbed dose into dose equivalent.

Pressure per cell is the MEDA noon value, 691.26 Pa, referenced to the median stop elevation and scaled with height using a scale height of 11,100 m. Sky view multiplies the result. It uses the same constants as the web app's telemetry.js.

entries.title: Sol
entries.summary: One Martian day (24 h 39 min 35 s).
body: Rover timelines count sols since landing. Perseverance landed on sol 0. The patch data covers sols 1349 to 1368 (December 2024). The Rovers tab plots odometry against sol.

entries.title: Local mean solar time (LMST)
entries.summary: Clock time of day at a spot on Mars.
body: Mars's day is divided into 24 'Mars hours' of about 61.7 minutes. The weather charts use hours 0 to 24 and mark the planned EVA start at 11:00 LMST, when the ground is about -15 to -4 C.

entries.title: Odometry
entries.summary: Distance a rover has driven.
body: Cumulative path length from the rover's wheel counts, reported in the MMGIS waypoints. The Rovers tab plots elevation against odometry (km) and odometry against sol.

entries.title: Traverse and stops
entries.summary: The rover's path, and the five places the EVA plan uses.
body: The traverse is the sequence of waypoints a rover has driven. The 'stops' are five real Perseverance parking spots chosen from rover photo coverage: 63_3564 (sols 1349-1351), 63_4462 (1354), 64_0 (1357), 64_1568 (1360-1362) and 64_2278 (1366-1368). All lie within 559 m of each other.

entries.title: EVA route
entries.summary: A stand-in walking route through the stops.
body: A slope-cost loop through the five stops (8 m steps, never above 20 degrees), included only so the explorer has a line to draw. The real planner lives in the Marswalk web app. Toggle it with 'EVA route' in the toolbar.

entries.title: Planning grid and the patch
entries.summary: The 2 x 2 km area the whole project is built around.
body: The patch is centred at 18.4593 N, 77.2690 E on the west rim of Jezero crater. The planning grid has 527 x 500 cells of 3.80 x 4.00 m; x is metres east and z metres south of the centre, row 0 is north. The site layers are drawn inside the dotted patch outline.

entries.title: Latitude, longitude and the map grid
entries.summary: How positions and the graticule are measured.
body: Positions are planetocentric degrees, east positive. The map is equirectangular: longitude is scaled by cos(latitude) at the view centre so shapes stay true near the middle of the screen. The Grid toggle draws the graticule. Type 'lat, lon' in the toolbar to jump to a place.

entries.title: No data
entries.summary: Pixels that hold no measurement.
body: Shown as transparent on the map and as 'no data' in the Probe. Scalar layers store it as NaN; CRISM tiles store it as the value 65535; images treat 0 as no data.

entries.title: Display range and stretch
entries.summary: The low and high values the colours span.
body: Each layer starts with its 2nd to 98th percentile as the range, so a few extreme pixels don't wash out the map. 'Stretch to view' recomputes it from the pixels on screen; 'Reset' returns to the default; or type your own.

entries.title: Stepped colours
entries.summary: Colours in 5 flat steps instead of a smooth gradient.
body: The web app draws its overlays in 5 levels, never as soft gradients. Tick 'Stepped (5 levels)' on a layer to get the same look.

entries.title: Pearson r and Spearman rho
entries.summary: Numbers the Compare tab uses to say how two layers relate.
body: Pearson r measures how well a straight line fits (-1 to +1). Spearman rho compares rank orders, so it also catches curved but steadily rising relationships. Both are computed on a 256 x 256 lattice over the view or region. Correlation is not cause: two layers can both depend on a third.

entries.title: Levels of detail and tiles
entries.summary: How the map stays fast from planet to 1 m.
body: Each raster has a pyramid of 2x averaged copies, cut into 512 px tiles. Only visible tiles at about one data pixel per screen pixel are coloured, in nearest-first order, while a coarser copy stands in. The status bar shows ms per frame and how many tiles are cached or queued.

entries.title: Layers panel
entries.summary: List of all 23 rasters with on/off, opacity, colours and range.
body: Layers are grouped Global, Jezero region and Site 2 km, finest on top. Tick to show, click to edit: opacity, colour map, range, hillshade and relief (DEMs only), stepped. The histogram shows the pixels on screen under the colour bar. 'Zoom to' flies to the layer's footprint.

entries.title: Probe tab
entries.summary: Every layer's value under the cursor.
body: Move over the map. The table lists each layer covering that point, finest first, with its pixel size, plus the best elevation (from the finest DEM there). Values are archive values at the nearest pixel; images show grey level.

entries.title: Profile tab
entries.summary: Elevation along a line you draw.
body: Choose 'Profile' in the toolbar and drag a line. Elevation is taken from the finest DEM under each sample and coloured by source: HiRISE (white), CTX (cyan), 100-200 m, or MOLA (orange). A second layer can be drawn on the right axis. It reports climb, descent and steepest grade.

entries.title: Compare tab and Region
entries.summary: Scatter plot of one layer against another.
body: Pick two layers and an area: the current view, or a box drawn with the 'Region' tool. The plot is a log-density scatter with a least-squares line, and summary statistics (mean, median, percentiles) sit below.

entries.title: Rovers tab
entries.summary: Perseverance and Curiosity drive history.
body: Waypoint count, sol range and distance driven for each rover, plus elevation along the drive and odometry by sol. 'Show' flies the map to the track. Perseverance has 708 waypoints; Curiosity's track is at Gale crater.

entries.title: Weather tab
entries.summary: MEDA temperature and pressure by Mars hour.
body: Air and ground temperature (C) and surface pressure (Pa), median per local hour, for the typical day and for each of the eight sols. Ground ranges about -82 to -4 C, air -75 to -40 C. Pressure at noon is 691.26 Pa. A few sun-heated hours survive in single sols; use the typical day for modelling.

entries.title: Overlays and toolbar toggles
entries.summary: Grid, Labels, Rovers, EVA route, Footprints, Credits.
body: Grid: lat/lon graticule and scale bar. Labels: named features at planet scale and approximate landing sites. Rovers: Perseverance (cyan) and Curiosity (yellow) tracks. EVA route: the stand-in loop and numbered stops. Footprints: outlines of every layer's coverage. Credits: the data credit of each visible layer, on the map.

entries.title: Go to bookmarks
entries.summary: Jump menu in the toolbar.
body: Whole planet, Jezero crater, Marswalk patch, Jezero west rim + delta, Isidis + Syrtis, Gale crater, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris and Hellas Planitia. Search any of these by name to fly there.
